legend: Eddard and his secret partner believe arrays should be symmetric, and any asymmetric array is worthless. So, they defined a function V(a)%%ZSMJ0%% as the value of array a%%ZSMJ1%% as follows:
If the array is symmetric*, V(a)%%ZSMJ2%% is equal to the sum of all elements in a%%ZSMJ3%%.
Given an array a%%ZSMJ5%%, calculate ∑nl=1∑nr=lV(a[l..r])%%ZSMJ6%%, where a[l..r]%%ZSMJ7%% is the subarray of a%%ZSMJ8%% from index l%%ZSMJ9%% to r%%ZSMJ10%%.
Since the answer can be too large, print it modulo 109+7%%ZSMJ11%%.

* A symmetric array is an array that stays the same when reversed. More formally, in a symmetric array a%%ZSMJ12%% of n%%ZSMJ13%% integers, ai=an+1−i%%ZSMJ14%% for 1≤i≤n%%ZSMJ15%%. For example, the arrays [1,3,1],[5,9,9,5],[25]%%ZSMJ16%% are symmetric, while [1,2],[4,6,4,4]%%ZSMJ17%% are not.
input: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases t%%ZSMJ18%% (1≤t≤104)%%ZSMJ19%%. The description of the test cases follows.
The first line of each test case contains the array length n%%ZSMJ20%% (1≤n≤106)%%ZSMJ21%%.
The second line of each test case contains n%%ZSMJ22%% integers a1,a2,...,an%%ZSMJ23%% (1≤ai≤109)%%ZSMJ24%%.
It is guaranteed that the sum of n%%ZSMJ25%% over all test cases does not exceed 106%%ZSMJ26%%.
output: For each test case, print the answer modulo 109+7%%ZSMJ27%%.
note: In the first test case, the subarrays of [1,2,1]%%ZSMJ28%% are {[1],[2],[1],[1,2],[2,1],[1,2,1]}%%ZSMJ29%%.
Only [1],[2],[1],[1,2,1]%%ZSMJ30%% are symmetric, so the answer is their sum: (1)+(2)+(1)+(1+2+1)=8%%ZSMJ31%%.
